title: Watch Off by Under 10 Miles. Why Split the £20,000?｜Curio Archive
description:
His watch's error at sea was only a third of the limit. So why couldn't it win the full £20,000?
For anyone who loves the history of science and wonders how "accurate" differs from "can be made again."

In 1714, Britain offered £20,000 for a way to work out longitude on a ship at sea. Clockmaker John Harrison produced a portable marine watch, and his son William took it on two voyages, to Jamaica and to Barbados. In 1765, Parliament wrote the Barbados trial into an act, but it also split the prize into two halves, each with its own conditions.

This episode follows the records in order: the three-tier prize, "one degree apart means about four minutes at noon," William's five-month wait at Portsmouth, the Jamaica voyage, taking the watch apart in front of the men the Board sent, the land trial at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, Harrison's pamphlet in reply, and finally the "forty-eight years" Parliament wrote down in 1773.

Two things up front: ten geographical miles is the judgment the 1765 act adopted; we did not recompute it from the logbooks. Harrison's criticism of the Board and of the astronomer Nevil Maskelyne is his own side's account.
